description: We are a team of curious minds, creative thinkers, and aspiring innovators excited to explore the world of space science and technology through the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
OrbitPulse is an interactive astronaut self-health monitoring tool, built as a Python notebook, for long-duration missions where help from the ground is delayed. It tracks eight daily indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood and exercise. Each indicator is colour-coded as normal, caution or alert. It also pulls recent solar flare and solar energetic particle events from NASA’s CCMC DONKI space-weather service and turns them into a daily radiation hazard index.

Crew members get a 30-day trend dashboard, an interactive body map showing which organ systems are affected, and a daily check-in. For every out-of-range reading, the check-in explains why it can happen in space and suggests what to do. It flags when to contact the flight surgeon. A health score, streaks and badges encourage daily use.

This addresses the challenge by giving astronauts a clear, visual way to assess and act on their own health. It matters because Moon and Mars crews will need to manage their health autonomously, and linking vitals to the radiation environment supports earlier detection of problems. Crew vitals are synthetic demo data, and the reference ranges are not medical advice.
details:
What it does and how it works

OrbitPulse is an interactive Python notebook that helps astronauts monitor their own health on long-duration missions. It works in five steps:

  1. Space-weather data: It pulls the last 30 days of solar flares and solar energetic particle (SEP) events from NASA’s CCMC DONKI service. It weights each event (X-class flares count most, then M, then C, and SEP events count heavily) and combines them into a daily radiation hazard index rated Low, Elevated or High.
  2. Vitals tracking: It tracks eight daily indicators: heart rate, systolic blood pressure, SpO₂, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep, mood and exercise. Each has a normal range and a caution range. Anything outside the caution range is an alert.
  3. Dashboards: A 30-day trend dashboard shows each indicator with its normal-range band and colour-coded points. An interactive body map lets the user hover over the brain, lungs, heart, blood, core/immune system and bones/muscle to see each one’s status, why it is affected in space and what to do.
  4. Daily check-in: An interactive form lets the astronaut enter the day’s values and click “Evaluate my health”. Every out-of-range reading comes with a short explanation (for example, fluid shifts in microgravity) and a concrete action. Red readings trigger an alert to contact the flight surgeon. High solar activity triggers a reminder to follow the radiation-shelter protocol.
  5. Motivation: A daily health score, green-day streaks and badges (Mission Fit, Bone Guardian, Sleep Master, Steady Mind) encourage consistent monitoring and exercise.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Supports crew autonomy when communication with Earth is delayed, as on Moon and Mars missions.
  • Links the space environment to physiology, so the astronaut can see how radiation relates to heart rate, sleep and mood.
  • Gives plain-language explanations and next steps instead of raw numbers, which reduces guesswork under stress.
  • Helps catch problems early through trends and a clear escalation path.
  • Covers physical and behavioural health in one view.

The intended impact is safer, more self-reliant crews on future deep-space missions. The same approach could also adapt to remote, isolated settings on Earth, such as polar stations and submarines.

Tools and technologies

  • Language and environment: Python in Google Colab / Jupyter
  • Data: NASA CCMC DONKI API (ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI-API) via requests
  • Analysis: pandas and numpy
  • Visualisation: plotly for the trend dashboard, body map and score chart, and matplotlib for the radiation chart
  • Interface: ipywidgets for the interactive check-in
  • Demo slides: PptxGenJS
  • Hardware: None required. It runs in a browser or on a laptop, so it is easy to deploy.
  • AI assistance: The code was generated with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic), as disclosed in the notebook.

Creativity

  • The body map turns abstract numbers into an intuitive picture of which organ systems need attention.
  • It couples live NASA space-weather data to crew health indicators, rather than treating vitals in isolation.
  • Gamification, such as streaks and badges, addresses the real problem of keeping crews engaged with routine self-monitoring.
  • Every alert pairs a “why” with an “action”, which makes it an educational coach and not just a monitor.
  • A dark mission-control look with a consistent traffic-light colour scheme makes status readable at a glance.

Factors considered

  • Realistic space health risks: microgravity fluid shifts, bone and muscle loss, radiation exposure, disrupted sleep and isolation.
  • Safety: A clear escalation path for red alerts, and caution-level readings prompt re-measurement.
  • Usability: Colour coding, hover details and one-click evaluation keep it simple under mission workload.
  • Reliability: The tool handles API failures gracefully and falls back to demo values if NASA data is unavailable.
  • Ethics and transparency: Crew vitals are synthetic demo data, the reference ranges are general values and not medical advice, and the use of AI assistance is disclosed.
  • Future work: Real wearable and biosensor integration, personalised baselines per astronaut, predictive alerts from radiation forecasts, and an offline mode for deep space.
